title: A Communication-Theoretic Framework for LLM Agents: Cost-Aware Adaptive Reliability
claim: A single tunable router traces a quality-cost frontier that beats every fixed technique, gaining quality at equal cost or cutting cost at equal quality.
layout: 2 panels, left scatter-curve with annotated arrows, right ranked dot-plot list
description: Two-panel results figure. Panel (a) is a scatter and line plot of mean quality against normalized cost (1x to 8x a single call). A bold blue curve with a light bootstrap band, labeled Semantic-KNN router (ours), rises steeply and then flattens near 0.87. Grey dots show the fixed techniques. An orange dot marks the cross-validated best fixed technique. A star marks the per-task oracle, and hollow markers show other routers. Two black arrows are annotated '+6.8% quality at the same cost' (vertical) and '55.7% lower cost at the same quality' (horizontal), with lambda labels at 3 and 38. Panel (b) is a ranked dot plot of 20 fixed techniques with confidence intervals and a cost column on the right. Vertical orange and blue lines mark the best fixed technique and the router. A marker legend runs along the bottom.
caption: Cost-aware router versus fixed choices on the 300-item hard split (Ollama-cloud trio: Nemotron-Nano-3 30B and Devstral-Small-2 24B as channels, GLM-5.1 as judge; three generation repeats per task; 5-fold stratified cross-validation). (a) Mean quality versus normalized cost ρ, in multiples of one uncoded call. Blue: the router as its knob λ is swept, with a 95% bootstrap band. Gray: the 20 fixed techniques. Orange: the cross-validated best fixed technique. Star: per-task oracle. Hollow markers: other routing policies. Arrows mark the gain at matched cost (λ=3) and the cost reduction at matched quality (λ=38). (b) Every fixed technique by mean quality with its 95% bootstrap interval, and its normalized cost at right; vertical lines mark the cross-validated best fixed technique and the router at λ=3. Quality is the judge score (Sec. 4); Sec. 5.5 repeats the comparison under judge-free grading.
abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) rely on reliability techniques such as retry, majority voting, and self-consistency developed in parallel rather than within a common analytical framework. We observe that an LLM sampled at temperature $T$ is a discrete stochastic channel $p(y \mid x)$ in the sense of Shannon's coding theory, and use this identity as the entry point for such a framework. Each of these techniques is a special case of one of six classical reliability operators: diversity combining, hybrid retransmission, iterative generator-critic decoding, rateless sampling, structured redundant verification, and difficulty-adaptive routing. Within the framework we give two closed-form results, a noise-variance threshold above which uniform averaging beats quality-weighted averaging and a contractivity criterion for generator-critic refinement, and turn each into a design rule checkable before committing compute. We further introduce a cost-aware semantic-nearest-neighbor router whose single Lagrangian knob traverses the quality-cost frontier without retraining. Across six local and cloud channel configurations, no fixed model-technique-budget choice dominates. On a 300-item hard split of MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, the router occupies the empirical Pareto frontier: at matched quality its normalized cost is $\approx$56% lower than the best fixed technique, and at matched cost it improves quality by $\approx$7% (26% over single-shot decoding). Judge-free grading of 6,900 outputs confirms that the judge tracks correctness at the item level and that the router's advantage over a fixed policy persists at most cost settings; with internal reasoning enabled, the gain of external refinement shrinks but remains significant for our incremental-redundancy operator. These results argue for consolidating reliability techniques into a single tunable layer informed by channel coding.
